vignette:
Kwame is a 78-year-old Ghanaian-born man who has lived in the United States for the better part of four decades, working for the last eighteen years as a librarian at a mid-sized public library in a quiet midwestern city. He is married, soft-spoken, and widely regarded by colleagues as a man of careful habits and deep reserves of patience. He presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 69, describing himself, with characteristic understatement, as "no longer quite right inside."

The event that reorganised Kwame's inner life occurred several years ago when he was visiting family in Accra. He had gone with his nephew to a crowded open-air market on a Saturday morning - the kind of place he had known since childhood, loud and warm and dense with movement. A bomb detonated in the market's eastern corridor. Kwame was close enough to be thrown from his feet by the pressure wave. When he rose, the scene around him was one of smoke, screaming, and bodies. He helped carry a woman whose legs were no longer intact. He held her hand until she died. The market, the press of people, the ordinary Saturday noise - all of it had been the context of catastrophe, and his nervous system encoded every detail with terrible precision.

His memories of that morning are, as he describes them, almost unbearably clear - not faded with time but sharpened, as though the event is still in the process of happening somewhere inside him. The images replay like footage he cannot stop: the smoke thickening, the woman's face, the particular quality of the screaming. Because the memory retains this unprocessed, present-tense quality, it does not wait for Kwame to invite it. Something in his surroundings - a sound, a smell, a flash of movement at the edge of his vision - can collapse the distance between then and now without warning, returning him fully to the market corridor. This quality of the memory, its immediacy and its hair-trigger accessibility, means that a wide range of ordinary stimuli have become potent cues.

At work in the library, this is most visible. Certain conversation topics - violence, political extremism, suffering abroad - can arrive across the reference desk without warning, and when they do, the memory surfaces instantly and completely. Witnessing someone behave badly, even in the minor register of a patron being rude or a child knocking over a display, carries for Kwame a moral charge that connects, through some associative pathway he cannot fully articulate, to the senseless cruelty of that morning. The anniversary of the attack arrives each year as a period of particular dread. When these triggers activate the memory, Kwame has learned - or rather, his body has learned on his behalf - to withdraw. He avoids crowded places now: the shopping centres his wife frequents, the public events his colleagues invite him to, the busy parts of the library during peak hours. He drifts, sometimes, into a private interior world, a kind of willed dissociation that offers temporary relief from the present. And he has come to refuse situations that might generate happiness or hope, as though good feeling is a surface too thin to trust.

What Kwame has not fully recognised is the way his strategies have begun to sustain the very problem they were built to manage. By withdrawing from crowds and from positive engagement, he has narrowed his life to a set of controlled, low-stimulus environments - and within those environments, the absence of competing experience means the memory occupies more of the available space. The avoidance itself seems to keep the memory close, rehearsed, ready. And because he is always managing his exposure, always scanning for what might need to be escaped, the conditions that once triggered the memory now include almost any deviation from his carefully maintained routine. Ordinary disruptions - a patron raising their voice, an unexpected crowd in the periodicals section - have become triggers in part because avoidance has made the world feel perpetually unsafe.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was his wife's quiet, sustained grief over what she described as losing him to a room she could not enter. He arrived hoping, above all, to be less afraid of his own mind - and afraid, most of all, that it may already be too late.
